Just for my own clarity: the way I understood our conversation on this, the goal is to (e.g.) be able to DMA-xfer a large block of data which may span _many_ descriptors, but only rely on completion/notification of the _last_ descriptor in the list.

If we look at how `xfer_k_entry_blocking()` and `xfer_v_entry_blocking()` work today, that's exactly the model they're following. They only wait on the last descriptor to complete.

I think the main difference is today, `xfer_k_entry_blocking()` and `xfer_v_entry_blocking()` assume at most **one wrap** between enqueue and completion time. this is the one 'sub-optimal' aspect of this work IMO... a 'copy buffer' for when model->head_size != hw->baked_head_size. Explanation:
```
  The FPGA image and HBM layout are baked for head_size = 128. HW reads Q with a fixed 128-element-per-
head stride, regardless of the model's actual head_size.                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                  
  For gpt-oss with head_size = 64, the model writes qs_for_attn at a 64-element-per-head stride. If you pointed
 HW at that buffer, every Q-head pointer past head 0 would be at the wrong offset — HW would read into the
 next head's data, mis-strided across all heads.                       
                                                                                                                                                  
 So we keep two parallel Q buffers:
  
  - qs_for_attn: model-native, n_heads * head_size (=n_heads * 64 for gpt-oss). Owned by SW; SW attention reads it unchanged.                     
  - hw_qs_for_attn: HW-shaped, n_heads * hw_baked_head_size (= n_heads * 128). Only allocated when need_q_padding = (head_size != hw_baked_head_size) is true (a static_option, so zero overhead for head_size==128 models).                                                      
                            
launch_hw_attention (self_attention.hpp:520-533) refreshes hw_qs_for_attn from qs_for_attn right before each
 HW dispatch: per head, copy the model's 64 elements into the 128-cell HW slot and zero-fill the upper 64. 
prepare_hw_attention (~line 478) points HW's activation pointers at hw_qs_for_attn when padding is needed, 
and the matmul template uses n_heads * hw_baked_head_size as the contraction size (self_attention.hpp:495) 
so HW's stride matches the padded buffer.

  Net effect: SW attention stays exact (reads native-stride qs_for_attn); HW attention sees a buffer shaped 
exactly the way the FPGA expects, with the unused upper half zeroed so it contributes nothing to the dot 
products.
```

Below are the findings of investigation:

>   The shard-creation paths only fire when:
>   - Boundary path: trailing = first_trailing falls within the edge's token range. For a fresh new edge with shards.empty(), this would create a shard at the boundary
>   base.
>   - Leaf-trailing path: n->children.empty() AND trailing_tokens >= 4 (gof_tokens). Same — would create if no shard at that base exists yet.

>   For the EAGLE to be the one entering this block "first" on a path that creates (rather than reuses) a shard, the EAGLE has to be the one extending a leaf edge into >=
>    4 trailing tokens past a boundary, on an edge whose shards vector doesn't already include that shard.
> 
>   With draft_tree_max_width = 1 (the default — src/tron/generation/speculate.cpp:24), drafts form a chain off the accepted-path leaf. But the actual sequence of events
>   is:
> 
>   1. exact samples: extends the accepted leaf edge by 1 token. exact's compute_forward_args walks the leaf edge with edge.dirty=true. Creates any new shards (correctly
>   sized for 32 layers). Sets edge.dirty=false.
>   2. EAGLE drafts: hangs off the new tip. EAGLE's compute_forward_args walks the same leaf edge — but edge.dirty is now false (exact just cleared it), so EAGLE doesn't
>   enter the block on that edge. EAGLE then walks the draft's own edge, which is short and never triggers leaf-trailing creation.
> 
>   So in practice, the exact always touches the accepted leaf edge first (because sampling is what grows it), and the EAGLE never creates shards.

Root cause is an eligibility/plan inconsistency: `use_hw_attn_for_this_model()` is a
pure runtime flag, and the compile-time `model_shape_is_hwattn_eligible()` checks
`head_size ∈ {64,128}` and `n_kv_heads` but **not** `n_heads`. `max_shards_for_emem`
returns 0 exactly when `n_heads > 128`. So a head_size-128, small-`n_kv_heads`,
high-GQA model with `n_heads > 128` is eligible + flag-on → `configure_hw_attention`
sets the HW layer mask → descent marks HW ranges → `construct_hw_plan` hits
`physical_shards_per_pass == 0` and silently returns an empty plan. The SW path then
runs only `sw_required` for those HW-offloaded (non-sliding) layers, so the
HW-covered tokens are computed by neither path → wrong attention output.

- `use_hw_attn_for_this_model()` now returns `false` when
  `max_shards_for_emem(n_heads, head_size, shard_tokens) == 0`. That predicate is the
  single lever gating `configure_hw_attention`'s HW mask, so the whole model becomes
  SW-only consistently — the real fallback the old log line only promised.
- The now-unreachable `physical_shards_per_pass == 0` branch in `construct_hw_plan`
  becomes `TRON_ASSERT(physical_shards_per_pass > 0, …)` (always-on) instead of a
  silent `return`, so any future mask/plan inconsistency aborts loudly rather than
  zeroing output.

xfer_gofs does some avoidable per-call work on the prefill critical path (a 4096-token 36-layer prefill runs this ~4608 times):

- gof.cpp:37 — the ctor memsets the whole batch allocation (up to 128 KiB), but in the common 8-head/128-head-size config the populate loops below overwrite every byte. Zeroing is only needed for the padded regions (kv_head_size < HW_BAKED_HEAD_SIZE, n_kv_heads < 8/odd). ~576 MB of dead stores per long prefill plus cache pollution.
- gof.cpp:256+ — six heap vectors per call (pieces/specs/bases/fetchers/qdatas/qlens); the sibling xfer_gof uses fixed stack arrays. Sizes are bounded by coalesce_gofs*(1+FETCHERS_PER_DEVICE), so stack arrays work here too.
- gof.cpp:278 — the std::sort of pieces is avoidable: emit K in fetcher order and V fetcher-major and the vector is sorted by construction.

Related, one level down: the V populate at gof.cpp:333 is piece-major, so v_head_fn runs its full head gather into the shared v_buf once per (fetcher,pos,head) — 1024 calls per GOF vs 32 in the gof::populate path this replaces — and the caller reads only head_size/32 of each gather. Inverting to (gof,pos,head)-outer and scattering with the packed writes shuffle_v_entry_padded already implements removes the 32x. That also matters for correctness margin: v_buf is per-(gal,position) but layer-agnostic while staging_busy is per-(gal,layer), so two workers batching different layers of one gal race on v_buf — a pre-existing window, but this widens it ~32x.

Two decode-path costs in the drain helpers:

- Here (and wait_for_coop_gof at :2993): the std::vector<gof_coop_task> is constructed and reserved before checking whether the coop queue has anything. These run from the hw_q_released_layer spin and begin_attention_job — per worker, per layer, per decode token — and the queue is almost always empty there, so this adds a malloc/free per spin iteration where the old code try_dequeued with zero allocation. Try-dequeue the first task before allocating (early-return on empty) and collect into a fixed std::array — task_budget is bounded by max(4, coalesce_gofs).
- gof_rodeo_impl_batch (:3114) re-asserts the kv_complete_fn condition fire_gof_rodeo already asserted on identical inputs. TRON_ASSERT is compiled into release, so every decode-path GOF completion pays 8 std::function invocations instead of 4. Keep one copy.
